statement: Every [continuous](c:continuous-function) real-valued function on a nonempty [compact space](c:compact-space) attains a maximum and a minimum.
conclusion: There are points $a, b \in X$ with $f(a) \le f(x) \le f(b)$ for every $x \in X$.

formal.difference: The declaration gives the minimum only, for a function continuous on a compact set with values in a linear order with closed lower rays. The maximum is the separate declaration IsCompact.exists_isMaxOn.

proofs.name: Compact image
proofs.slogan: The image of the compact space is a compact set of reals, and such a set contains its supremum and infimum.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. An empty space has no maximum, so the hypothesis $X \neq \emptyset$ is necessary; the proof uses it only to make the image nonempty.

roles.why: Continuity pulls an [open cover](c:open-cover) of the image back to an open cover of $X$.
A nonempty space has a nonempty image, so the supremum and infimum exist.

steps.slogan: Push the [compact space](c:compact-space) forward to its [image](c:image) under $f$.
steps.detail: Let $\{V_i\}$ be an [open cover](c:open-cover) of $f(X)$. The preimages $f^{-1}(V_i)$ are open because $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function), and they cover $X$. Finitely many of them cover $X$, so the matching finitely many $V_i$ cover $f(X)$. Hence $f(X)$ is compact.

steps.slogan: Show that the compact image is a [closed](c:closed-set) and [bounded set](c:bounded-set) of reals.
steps.detail: The open intervals $(-n, n)$ cover $f(X)$ and finitely many suffice, so $f(X)$ is bounded. A compact subset of the Hausdorff space $\mathbb{R}$ is closed, so $f(X)$ is closed.

steps.slogan: Take the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) and the infimum of the nonempty bounded image.
steps.detail: The image is nonempty because $X$ is nonempty, and it is bounded. The completeness of the [real numbers](c:real-number) gives $M = \sup f(X)$ and $m = \inf f(X)$.

steps.slogan: Find the supremum and the infimum inside the closed image.
steps.detail: Every neighborhood of $M$ meets $f(X)$, so $M$ lies in the closure of $f(X)$, which is $f(X)$ because the image is [closed](c:closed-set). Hence $M = f(b)$ for some $b \in X$. In the same way $m = f(a)$ for some $a \in X$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: The function must be continuous so that preimages of open sets are open.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness is the property that passes from the space to its image.
concepts.c:open-cover: The image is shown compact through an open cover and its preimage cover.
concepts.c:image: The proof studies the set of values $f(X)$ instead of the function.
concepts.c:closed-set: A closed set of reals contains the limits of its points, so it contains its supremum.
concepts.c:bounded-set: A bounded set of reals has a finite supremum and infimum.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: The supremum is the candidate for the maximum value.
concepts.c:real-number: Completeness of the reals supplies the supremum.

source.note: mathlib takes the compact image (IsCompact.image_of_continuousOn) and its least element (IsCompact.exists_isLeast).

proofs.name: Local bounds and a reciprocal
proofs.slogan: Bound the function near each point, keep finitely many bounds, then show that the supremum is a value.
proofs.scope: The maximum; the minimum follows when the proof is applied to $-f$. The proof needs $X$ nonempty for the supremum to exist. Steps 1 to 3 alone prove boundedness; boundedness does not give attainment, and steps 4 and 5 supply it.

roles.why: Continuity gives a bound near each point, and it makes the reciprocal $1/(M - f)$ continuous.
[Compactness](c:compact-space) reduces the cover by bounded neighborhoods to a finite cover.
A nonempty set of values has a supremum.

steps.slogan: Cover the space by bounded neighborhoods.
steps.detail: For each $x \in X$, [continuity](c:continuous-function) at $x$ gives an open neighborhood $U_x$ on which $|f(y) - f(x)| < 1$, so $|f| < |f(x)| + 1$ on $U_x$. The sets $U_x$ form an [open cover](c:open-cover) of $X$.

steps.slogan: Select a finite subcover of the neighborhood cover.
steps.detail: Because $X$ is [compact](c:compact-space), finitely many points $x_1, \dots, x_n$ have neighborhoods $U_{x_1}, \dots, U_{x_n}$ that still cover $X$. This finiteness is derived here; it is not a hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Take the largest of the finitely many local bounds.
steps.detail: On $X$, $|f| \le \max_i (|f(x_i)| + 1)$; a [finite set](c:finite-set) of reals has a largest element because $n \ge 1$, which holds since $X$ is nonempty. So $f$ is a [bounded function](c:bounded-function) and $M = \sup f(X)$ is a [real number](c:real-number).

steps.slogan: Assume that $M$ is not a value and form the reciprocal $g = 1/(M - f)$.
steps.detail: If $f(x) < M$ for every $x$, then $g(x) = 1/(M - f(x))$ is defined, positive and [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $X$, because $M - f$ is continuous and never zero.

steps.slogan: Bound the reciprocal by steps 1 to 3 and contradict the choice of $M$.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 applied to $g$ give $g \le K$ for some $K > 0$. Then $M - f(x) \ge 1/K$, so $f \le M - 1/K$ on $X$, which contradicts $M = \sup f(X)$. So $M = f(b)$ for some $b$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity gives a bound near each point and keeps the reciprocal continuous.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness turns the local bounds into finitely many bounds.
concepts.c:open-cover: The bounded neighborhoods form the open cover that compactness reduces.
concepts.c:finite-set: Only a finite family of bounds has a largest member.
concepts.c:bounded-function: Boundedness makes the supremum a real number, not infinity.
concepts.c:real-number: The supremum exists because the reals are complete.

source.note: The classical proof by local boundedness and the reciprocal function, as in Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, theorem 4.16 and its exercise route; not the mathlib route.

statement: If $f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) and $y$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then $f(c) = y$ for some $c \in [a, b]$.

hypotheses.text: The domain is a closed [interval](c:interval) $[a, b]$ with $a \le b$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the image of $[a, b]$ contains $[f(a), f(b)]$, for a densely ordered, conditionally complete domain and an order-closed codomain. The case $f(b) \le f(a)$ is the separate declaration intermediate_value_Icc'.

proofs.name: Connected image
proofs.slogan: The interval is connected, so its image is connected, and a connected set of reals contains every value between two of its values.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for either order of $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.

roles.why: The two end values are points of the image, and $y$ lies between them.

steps.slogan: Show that the closed interval $[a, b]$ is a [connected space](c:connected-space).
steps.detail: Suppose $[a, b] = U \cup V$ with disjoint nonempty relatively open sets and $a \in U$. Let $s = \sup\{x : [a, x] \subseteq U\}$. Openness of $U$ and of $V$ near $s$ gives a contradiction, so no such split exists.

steps.slogan: Push the connected interval forward to its connected [image](c:image) under $f$.
steps.detail: If $f([a, b])$ were split by two disjoint relatively open sets, their preimages under the [continuous](c:continuous-function) $f$ would split $[a, b]$, which step 1 excludes.

steps.slogan: Show that the connected image holds every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.
steps.detail: If $y$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ but is not a value, the sets $\{t < y\}$ and $\{t > y\}$ split the image into two nonempty relatively open parts, against step 2. So $y = f(c)$ for some $c$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity is what makes the image connected.
concepts.c:interval: The interval is the connected domain of the function.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness is the property that passes from the domain to the image.
concepts.c:image: The proof studies the set of values $f([a, b])$.

proofs.name: Supremum of the lower set
proofs.slogan: Take the last point where $f$ is at most $y$ and show that $f$ equals $y$ there.
proofs.scope: The case $f(a) \le y \le f(b)$; the other case follows when the proof is applied to $-f$ and $-y$.

roles.why: The inequality $f(a) \le y$ puts $a$ in the set $S$, and $y \le f(b)$ controls the right end.
The bounded [interval](c:interval) makes $S$ bounded and keeps its supremum in $[a, b]$.
Continuity at $c$ passes both inequalities through the limits.

steps.slogan: Collect the points where $f$ stays at most $y$ into a set $S$.
steps.detail: Let $S = \{x \in [a, b] : f(x) \le y\}$. Because $f(a) \le y$, the point $a$ is in $S$, so $S$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Take the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) $c$ of the nonempty bounded set $S$.
steps.detail: The set $S$ is nonempty and bounded above by $b$, so the completeness of the [real numbers](c:real-number) gives $c = \sup S$, and $a \le c \le b$.

steps.slogan: Approach $c$ from inside $S$ to get $f(c) \le y$.
steps.detail: Choose $x_n \in S$ with $x_n \to c$. Then $f(x_n) \le y$ and [continuity](c:continuous-function) gives $f(c) = \lim f(x_n) \le y$.

steps.slogan: Approach $c$ from the right to get $f(c) \ge y$.
steps.detail: If $c = b$, then $f(c) = f(b) \ge y$. If $c < b$, the points $c + 1/n$ (for large $n$) are not in $S$, so $f(c + 1/n) > y$, and continuity gives $f(c) \ge y$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two inequalities into $f(c) = y$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $y \le f(c) \le y$, so $f(c) = y$ with $c \in [a, b]$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity at the supremum turns limits of inequalities into inequalities.
concepts.c:interval: The interval bounds the set $S$ and holds its supremum.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: The supremum of $S$ is the point where $f$ meets $y$.
concepts.c:real-number: Completeness of the reals supplies the supremum.

source.note: The classical least-upper-bound proof (Bolzano's proof as usually taught).

proofs.name: Bisection
proofs.slogan: Halve the interval again and again, keep a half whose end values straddle $y$, and take the common point.
proofs.scope: The case $f(a) \le y \le f(b)$; the other case follows from $-f$ and $-y$.

roles.why: The first interval has $f(a) \le y \le f(b)$, which starts the halving.
A closed bounded [interval](c:interval) can be halved into closed intervals whose lengths go to zero.
Continuity at the common point passes both end inequalities to the limit.

steps.slogan: Halve the current interval and keep a half whose end values straddle $y$.
steps.detail: Given $[a_n, b_n]$ with $f(a_n) \le y \le f(b_n)$, let $m$ be its midpoint. If $f(m) \le y$, keep $[m, b_n]$; otherwise keep $[a_n, m]$. The kept half has the same property.

steps.slogan: Repeat the halving to get nested intervals of length $(b - a)/2^n$.
steps.detail: The intervals $[a_n, b_n]$ are nested, $a_n$ increases, $b_n$ decreases and $b_n - a_n = (b - a)/2^n \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Take the common point $c$ of the nested intervals.
steps.detail: The bounded monotone sequences $a_n$ and $b_n$ converge in the [real numbers](c:real-number) to the same limit $c \in [a, b]$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit at both ends to get $f(c) = y$.
steps.detail: By [continuity](c:continuous-function), $f(c) = \lim f(a_n) \le y$ and $f(c) = \lim f(b_n) \ge y$, so $f(c) = y$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity at the common point turns the end inequalities into an equation.
concepts.c:interval: Closed intervals can be halved and nested.
concepts.c:real-number: Completeness of the reals gives the common point of the nested intervals.

source.note: The bisection proof, which is also the bisection method for root finding.
